<reason>A's decisive move was turning B's own "follow unmet need" standard into an empirical weapon: widely known, plausible facts about recess/PE/arts cuts and pandemic-era device distribution gave A a concrete, uncontested account of where the deficit actually lies, and B never disputed those facts—only argued they don't settle which specific school's next investment is better, without ever offering comparable grounding that digital deprivation is comparably widespread. B's case-by-case reframing was a legitimate CON strategy and B's closing landed a sharp, unanswered catch (A's stated override condition—requiring full sufficiency in physical/arts—is stricter than the "larger reachable deficit" rule A claimed convergence on in its own closing), which exposes real looseness in A's framework. But that catch is a narrow rule-consistency point, not a rebuttal of A's core empirical claim about where the general, default-case deficit sits, and B's own counterexamples (the bus-rider, the caregiver) remained anecdotal rather than systemic. A's clipped opening is a real execution cost, and A's closing somewhat oversells B's concessions, but across the full exchange A did more of the decisive comparative work by making the "default" question turn on documented, common-case facts rather than exceptions.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 move ([A2.2]-[A2.3]) applying B's own "follow the unmet need" criterion to argue it actually favors physical/arts programs, versus B's Closing catch ([B5.1]) showing A's stated override standard is stricter than the "larger reachable deficit" rule A claimed to share—these two exchanges were the debate's real hinge points, with A's landing earlier and shaping most of the debate, and B's landing last but on a narrower point.</best_rebuttal>
